title: “HUSBANDS, LOVE YOUR WIVES” — PAUL’S COMMAND WAS FAR MORE COSTLY THAN MANY ADMIT
paragraphs: “HUSBANDS, LOVE YOUR WIVES” — PAUL’S COMMAND WAS FAR MORE COSTLY THAN MANY ADMIT
We have argued for generations about what a wife owes her husband. But what if we have not trembled enough over what Christ commands a husband to become?
There is a frightening way to read the Bible.
You can underline the verses that give you authority and quietly skip the verses that crucify your ego.
You can memorize what Scripture says someone else should do for you while remaining strangely unfamiliar with what Scripture commands you to sacrifice for them.
And perhaps nowhere has this happened more painfully than in Christian conversations about marriage.
“Husbands, love your wives.”
We have heard it at weddings.
Printed it on plaques.
Placed it beneath smiling engagement photographs.
Turned it into marriage conference material.
It sounds warm.
Gentle.
Almost romantic.
Until you finish the sentence.
Because Paul did not merely write, “Husbands, love your wives.”
The Greek text of Ephesians 5:25 reads:
“Οἱ ἄνδρες, ἀγαπᾶτε τὰς γυναῖκας, καθὼς καὶ ὁ Χριστὸς ἠγάπησεν τὴν ἐκκλησίαν καὶ ἑαυτὸν παρέδωκεν ὑπὲρ αὐτῆς.”
“Husbands, love your wives, as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her.”
Read those final words again.
“ἑαυτὸν παρέδωκεν.”
“He gave Himself up.”
That changes everything.
Because Paul does not allow a husband to define love according to his personality, upbringing, culture, preferences, paycheck, masculinity, emotions, or convenience.
He points to Jesus.
Then he points toward the cross.
And essentially says:
Love her like that.
Suddenly this is not a decorative marriage verse anymore.
It is a death sentence for selfishness.
A man may provide money and still withhold himself.
He may pay every bill and still make his wife feel emotionally abandoned.
He may never commit adultery physically while allowing pornography, fantasy, flirtation, secrecy, or emotional distance to occupy territory in his heart that covenant love should guard.
He may know how to lead a meeting, manage employees, preach a sermon, quote Scripture, correct theology, and command respect...
and still have no idea how to make the woman sleeping beside him feel heard.
That should trouble us.
Because Paul does not tell husbands merely to rule their homes efficiently.
He commands them to love.
“ἀγαπᾶτε”—agapate.
It is a command.
Not a suggestion for naturally affectionate men.
Not an optional personality trait.
Not something dependent upon whether she is easy to love today.
And Paul refuses to leave “love” undefined.
He gives it a face.
Jesus Christ.
He gives it a shape.
Self-giving.
He gives it a direction.
Toward the beloved.
He gives it a cost.
Yourself.
This is where the verse becomes uncomfortable.
A husband can demand respect without dying to pride.
He can demand submission without surrendering selfishness.
He can demand peace while terrorizing the atmosphere with anger.
He can demand intimacy while neglecting tenderness.
He can demand that his wife listen while rarely asking what she is carrying.
He can demand biblical womanhood while conveniently constructing a version of biblical manhood that costs him almost nothing.
But you cannot imitate the Christ of Ephesians 5 without something in you dying.
Jesus did not love His bride from a safe distance.
He gave Himself.
The Lord of glory knelt.
The King served.
The sinless One carried what was not His.
The Shepherd laid down His life for sheep who wandered.
Christ's love was not merely spoken.
It bled.
And this matters because Christian headship can never biblically mean permission to become a household tyrant.

Jesus explicitly rejected the worldly pattern of greatness that “lords it over” others and instead pointed His disciples toward servanthood. The Son of Man Himself came not to be served, but to serve and to give His life as a ransom for many.
So whatever Christian leadership means, it cannot contradict Jesus.
A husband cannot say, “I am following Christ,” while using Scripture to frighten, humiliate, manipulate, control, sexually coerce, degrade, or silence his wife.
That is not Christlike leadership.
That is sin wearing religious vocabulary.
And Scripture never gives abuse sanctuary merely because the abuser can quote a verse.
Look again at Jesus.
The cross was not Christ forcing His bride to suffer for Him.
It was Christ giving Himself for His bride.
That distinction is enormous.
Paul does not say:
“Husbands, make sure your wives sacrifice enough for you.”
He says, in effect:
Look at Christ.
Now look at yourself.
That is the terrifying mirror.
Perhaps the question is no longer simply:
“Does my wife submit?”
Perhaps another question needs to enter the room:
“Does my wife recognize something of Jesus in the way I love her?”
Not perfection.
No husband is Christ.
No marriage perfectly displays the Gospel.
But direction matters.
When she is exhausted, does your strength become shelter or another demand?
When she speaks, do you listen to understand or merely wait for your opportunity to defend yourself?
When you are wrong, can you say the words some men seem almost physically incapable of saying?
“I was wrong.”
“I hurt you.”
“Please forgive me.”
No excuses attached.
No sermon afterward.
No explanation about why she caused your reaction.
Just repentance.
Because sometimes the most masculine thing a Christian husband can do is repent without protecting his ego.
Some men will fight strangers for their wives but will not fight the pride destroying intimacy inside their own homes.
They would take a bullet for her.
But will they put down the phone for her?
Will they abandon pornography for her?
Will they surrender the secret conversation?
Will they stop weaponizing silence?
Will they help when nobody applauds?
Will they listen to the same fear again because she is still healing?
Will they choose tenderness after a twelve-hour workday?
Will they pray with her when the marriage feels awkward?
Will they seek counsel before resentment becomes a graveyard?
Would you die for her?
Maybe.
But Christianity asks something that can sometimes feel even harder.
Will you die to yourself for her...
again tomorrow?
And the next morning?
And when nobody sees?
That is where romantic Christianity collides with cruciform Christianity.
The cross is dramatic when viewed from a distance.
Self-denial is painfully ordinary when lived in a kitchen.
Sometimes Christlike love looks like apologizing first.
Sometimes it looks like washing dishes.
Sometimes it looks like telling the truth about the money.
Sometimes it means refusing to hide your screen.
Sometimes it means learning what makes your wife afraid.
Sometimes it means remembering that motherhood is work.
Sometimes it means protecting time with her rather than giving everyone else the strongest version of yourself and bringing your family whatever remains.
Sometimes it means getting help because “this is just how I am” is not a fruit of the Spirit.
Sometimes it means admitting that your wife has spent years surviving the very man who promised before God to cherish her.
That sentence may hurt.
Let it.
Conviction is not condemnation when it drives us toward Christ.
There is grace here.
Massive grace.
Because this article is not about announcing that husbands are hopeless failures.
The Gospel does not expose sin merely to leave sinners naked beneath accusation.
Jesus exposes what He intends to redeem.
Maybe you have failed your wife.
Maybe badly.
Maybe you became your father without realizing it.
Maybe anger became normal.
Maybe affection disappeared.
Maybe work became your mistress.
Maybe pornography quietly trained your eyes to consume women rather than honor them.
Maybe you were physically present but emotionally unreachable.
Maybe she stopped telling you what hurts because experience taught her that honesty would become another argument.
Maybe she cried beside you...
and you slept.
And perhaps reading this is awakening memories you would rather bury.
Do not run.
This is where scandal can become grace.
Because Christianity is not the announcement that good husbands earn God's acceptance.
Christianity is the announcement that sinners can be reconciled to God through Jesus Christ.
The Husband who failed needs the Savior who did not.
Christ died for selfish husbands too.
For angry husbands.
For adulterous husbands.
For emotionally absent husbands.
For controlling husbands.
For proud husbands.
For men who discovered far too late how deeply they wounded someone they genuinely loved.
But grace does not say, “Remain there.”
Grace teaches us to repent.
Forgiveness is not God's permission to continue destroying people.
The Gospel pardons us and begins transforming us.
So maybe your next act of spiritual leadership is not giving your wife another Bible verse.
Maybe it is sitting beside her and asking:
“Where have I hurt you?”
Then remaining quiet long enough to hear the answer.
Not correcting her memory.
Not debating her wording.
Not explaining your intentions.
Listening.
And if what she describes is true...
repent.
Because your intention does not erase her wound.
And husbands, Scripture becomes even more sobering.
Peter commands husbands to live with their wives with understanding and honor them as fellow heirs of the grace of life, warning that failure here can affect their prayers.
Think about that.
A man can sound spiritual publicly while Heaven cares deeply about how he treats his wife privately.
God sees the tone nobody at church hears.
God sees the contempt hidden behind closed doors.
God sees the tears.
God sees the cold silence.
God sees whether Scripture is being used as medicine or as ammunition.
And God sees the husband who is genuinely trying too.
The man nobody praises.
The man breaking generational patterns he inherited.
The man learning tenderness at forty because nobody showed him tenderness at ten.
The man working hard, coming home exhausted, and still kneeling beside his children's beds.
The husband confessing temptation instead of feeding it secretly.
The man going to counseling.
The man learning to communicate.
The man choosing fidelity when opportunity whispers.
The man whose marriage is wounded but who refuses to stop praying, serving, repenting, growing, and hoping in Christ.
Brother...
keep going.
Your wife does not need you to become Jesus.
She needs you to keep becoming like Him.
And wives reading this—this passage is not permission to demand perfection from your husband either.
Marriage places two sinners in extraordinarily close proximity and commands them to practice covenant faithfulness under the lordship of Christ.
Both need grace.
Both need repentance.
Both need forgiveness.
Both need Jesus.
But Ephesians 5:25 speaks directly to husbands, and we should let its weight remain where Scripture places it.
“Husbands, love your wives.”
Not only when she admires you.
Not only when intimacy is easy.
Not only when finances are stable.
Not only when she looks like the woman in your wedding photographs.
Love the woman whose body has changed.
Love the woman carrying grief she struggles to explain.
Love the woman aging beside you.
Love the woman who knows your weaknesses and remained.
Love her when marriage becomes ordinary.
Love her when life becomes expensive.
Love her when children consume the schedule.
Love her when illness enters the house.
Love her when misunderstandings require patience.
Love her when you must choose between winning the argument and protecting the relationship.
And understand carefully what biblical love does not mean.
Christlike sacrifice does not require enabling sin.
It does not require hiding abuse.
It does not forbid boundaries, accountability, church discipline, counseling, legal protection, or seeking safety when someone is in danger.
The cross is never permission for evil.
Jesus' sacrificial love confronts sin in order to redeem, not preserve it.

But in an ordinary Christian marriage, something astonishing can happen when two people stop asking, “How little can I give and still call this covenant?” and begin asking, “How can Christ be seen in me here?”
A home can change.
Children notice.
They notice when Daddy apologizes to Mommy.
They notice when he honors her in public and private.
They notice whether masculinity means intimidation or protection.
They notice whether Christianity makes their father harsher...
or holier.
One day your son may treat a woman partly according to what he watched you normalize.
One day your daughter may evaluate a man's love partly through what love looked like in her childhood home.
That is not a small responsibility.
You are teaching even when you are not talking.
And maybe that is why this verse deserves to escape the wedding card and return to the cross.
“Husbands, love your wives.”
How much?
“καθὼς καὶ ὁ Χριστὸς...”
“As Christ...”
There is the standard.
Impossible in our own strength.
Necessary enough to drive us continually back to grace.
Because ultimately Ephesians 5 is bigger than marriage.
Marriage is pointing somewhere.
Toward Christ and His Church.
Earthly husbands fail.
Jesus does not.
Earthly spouses disappoint.
Jesus remains faithful.
Human covenant love sometimes fractures beneath sin.
Christ went to a cross for His people.
He took sinners who had nothing worthy enough to purchase redemption and paid the price Himself.
The Gospel is not that we finally became lovable enough for Jesus.
The Gospel is that while we were sinners, Christ died for us.
That is why a Christian husband does not love his wife merely because she has earned another day of affection.
He loves from the grace he himself has received.
Forgiven men learn to forgive.
Served men learn to serve.
Loved men learn to love.
And crucified pride makes room for resurrected marriages.
Maybe yours feels too damaged.
Maybe years have been wasted.
Maybe trust has been shattered.
Maybe there are consequences repentance cannot instantly remove.
Do not cheapen grace by pretending consequences disappear overnight.
Trust can take time to rebuild.
Some wounds require professional help.
Some marriages require serious intervention.
Some situations involving abuse require immediate safety and accountability.
But never confuse “difficult” with “beyond Christ.”
Jesus specializes in graves.
Resurrection is His territory.
Perhaps the first resurrection needed in your marriage is simply a dead man's pride finally surrendering.
So tonight...
before another sermon.
Before another marriage book.
Before correcting your wife.
Before explaining what she should change.
Go somewhere quiet.
Open Ephesians 5.
Read verse 25 slowly.
Then ask Jesus:
“Lord, where have I demanded what I have refused to give?”
And wait.
If He exposes something...
do not hide.
Repent.
Not because comments save anyone.
Only Christ saves.
But sometimes confession begins when pride finally stops pretending.

And if God has restored something in your marriage that once looked impossible, tell your testimony. Someone reading silently may desperately need evidence that repentance, forgiveness, wise help, perseverance, and the grace of Jesus Christ can still rebuild what sin nearly destroyed.
Not because every sentence is perfect, but because Ephesians 5:25 deserves another reading after the emotion settles.
Send it privately to the husband who is trying.
Send it to the wife who needs to know Scripture never gave her husband permission to become her tyrant.
But hear this clearly:
It does not purchase salvation.
It does not make Jesus love you more.
And we will not tell you that supporting Gospel Warrior replaces whatever convictions and responsibilities you have regarding giving through your local church or caring for people in need.
Scripture says:
“ἕκαστος καθὼς προῄρηται τῇ καρδίᾳ... μὴ... ἐξ ἀνάγκης”
Give as you have purposed in your heart—not under compulsion.
That matters to us.
So if you want to glorify God through helping Gospel-centered truth reach more people, prayerfully consider Gospel Warrior as one ministry you voluntarily support.
One share can place Scripture in front of a marriage quietly collapsing.
One tag can reach a man too proud to ask for help.
One saved article can be reopened after an argument.
One honest comment can make another wounded believer realize they are not alone.
One invitation to follow can bring someone into daily contact with the Word of God.
Do it prayerfully.
Do it freely.
Do it because you believe Gospel truth is worth helping carry farther—not because anyone frightened you into giving.
And husbands...
before you leave this article thinking about another man who needed to read it...
come back one final time.
“Husbands, love your wives.”
The command was never cheap.
The pattern was never comfortable.
The standard was never your father, your culture, your favorite preacher, your masculinity, or the other husbands around you.
The standard standing before you has nail scars.
And perhaps the greatest thing your family will ever remember about your strength is not how loudly you commanded the house...
but how deeply Jesus taught you to lay yourself down in love.
Before asking whether she has become the wife you wanted, stand beneath the cross and ask whether you are becoming the husband Christ commanded.
